40-005.r: Irrigated share of cropped area 2011: Haryana 83.90% (highest of options), UP 72.76%, MP 28.20%, Maharashtra 16.78%. Variant answer: Punjab (99.6%, 2015-16).

40-007.r: Micro-irrigation → reduces fertilizer/nutrient loss and checks falling groundwater; it is not the only means in dry-land farming (answer 1 and 3).

40-008.r: Life-saving / Protective irrigation → irrigation at P.W.P. (Permanent Wilting Point), when soil moisture can no longer sustain plants.

40-009.r: Tubewell irrigation grew most spectacularly in the Saryupar Plain → because canals are lacking there.

40-010.r: Maximum area irrigated by tubewells → Uttar Pradesh (74.1% of its irrigated area, Statistical Diary of UP 2024).
40-010.h: UP = tubewell state: the same answer for tubewell, tube well and well+tubewell questions.

40-011.r: Largest area under tube-well irrigation (2022-23) → Uttar Pradesh.

40-012.r: Largest area under tubewell + well irrigation → Uttar Pradesh: 10402 thousand ha by tubewells, 1269 thousand ha by wells (Statistical Diary 2024).

40-013.r: Groundwater for irrigation (2024, billion cubic m): Uttar Pradesh 41.15 > Maharashtra 15.07 > West Bengal 8.99 > Assam 2.06 → order 4, 3, 2, 1.

40-014.r: Garland Canal System → proposed by Captain Dineshaw J. Dastur; river interlinking first proposed by M. Visvesvaraya, later K.L. Rao.
40-014.t: Don't confuse Dastur (Garland Canal) with Visvesvaraya or K.L. Rao (river interlinking proposals).

40-015.r: Pioneer of irrigation works in South India → Sir Arthur Cotton (British irrigation engineer).

40-016.r: Maximum irrigation potential in India → created through Minor Projects (CCA up to 2,000 ha each; dug wells, tubewells).

40-017.r: Farakka canal capacity → 40,000 cusecs; Farakka Barrage (Murshidabad, West Bengal, 1975) keeps Kolkata Port navigable via Bhagirathi-Hooghly.

40-018.r: Mangalam Irrigation Project → Kerala (Palakkad district, Bharath Puzha river system).

40-019.r: Saran irrigation canal → drawn from the Gandak (740 m barrage at Balmiki Nagar).

40-020.r: Indira Gandhi Canal → starts at Harike Barrage (Satluj-Beas confluence, Firozpur, Punjab); begun 1958; main canal 649 km; irrigates western Rajasthan.
40-020.h: Harike = meeting point of Satluj and Beas.

40-024.r: Indira Gandhi Canal water supply → Satluj, Beas and Ravi (not Chenab).

40-025.r: Pong dam on Beas → keeps winter flow in Indira Gandhi Canal; Beas project is joint: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan.

40-026.r: Gang Canal → oldest canal system of Rajasthan, built 1927 by Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner; from Satluj at Hussainiwala (Ferozepur).

40-027.r: Upper Bari Doab Canal → Ravi; Sirhind Canal → Sutlej; Gurgaon Canal → Yamuna; Indira Gandhi Canal → Sutlej, Ravi, Beas. Gang Canal built 1927.
40-027.h: Bari Doab = land between Beas and Ravi.

40-029.r: Sharda Tributary Command Development Project aims: more farm output, multiple cropping (land-use change), better land management → all three. CADP began December 1974.

40-030.r: Not true: Ghaggar water used in Indira Gandhi Canal. True: Narmada rises near Amarkantak; Nizam Sagar on Manjra; Penganga is a Godavari tributary.

40-031.r: Lower Ganga Canal → taken out of the Ganga at Narora (Bulandshahr); completed 1878.

40-033.r: Hariyali scheme (27 January 2003, PM Vajpayee) → wasteland development under watershed management; variant answer: water management.

40-035.r: Integrated Watershed Development benefits: prevents soil runoff, rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge, regenerates vegetation; not river linking (1, 3, 4).

40-036.r: DPAP and Desert Development Programme → Ministry of Rural Development (Dept of Land Resources; merged into IWMP 2008); watershed project for rainfed areas not Rural Development → no pair correct.

40-037.r: Drip irrigation advantages → less weeds, less soil erosion, saves water and fertilizer; soil salinity reduction not counted (answer 1 and 3).

40-038.r: Buckingham Canal → Coromandel Coast; 796 km freshwater navigation canal from Kakinada (Andhra Pradesh) to near Chidambaram (Tamil Nadu), via Chennai.

40-039.r: Largest water-consuming sector in India → Agriculture (irrigation); rainfall gives about 3880 billion cubic metres of water a year.

40-040.r: Chambal Canal Irrigation Project → Yamuna basin (Chambal is a Yamuna tributary) and so the larger Ganga basin; the book accepts both (b) and (c).

41-001.r: Sardar Sarovar Dam (163 m) → Narmada, near Navagam, Gujarat; beneficiary states: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan.

41-004.r: Four-state partnership project → Sardar Sarovar (Narmada); multipurpose: irrigation, drinking water, hydroelectric power.

41-005.r: Sardar Sarovar Dam: the book says Madhya Pradesh gets the maximum benefit of Narmada water.

41-006.r: Medha Patekar → led opposition to Sardar Sarovar Project; founded the Narmada Bachao Andolan.

41-007.r: Not on Narmada: Ban Sagar (on Son). Bargi, Omkareshwar, Indira Sagar → Narmada (part of its series of 30 major dams).

41-009.r: Harsud town (Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh) → submerged in 2004 by Indira Sagar Dam.

41-010.r: Omkareshwar project → Narmada river, Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh.
41-010.h: Khandwa pair on Narmada: Indira Sagar and Omkareshwar.

41-011.r: Narmada Bachao Andolan → opposes raising the height of Sardar Sarovar Dam; Narmada Valley Project: Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra.

42-001.r: Bhakra Nangal → joint project of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan; two dams (Bhakra and Nangal) on the Satluj.

43-001.r: Oldest hydropower plant → Darjeeling, West Bengal (1897); Shivasamudram on Kaveri, Karnataka (1902) is second oldest and the answer among options.

43-003.r: Cauvery River Water Dispute → Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Puducherry.
43-003.h: Three states + one UT share the Cauvery.

44-001.r: Nagarjuna Sagar Dam → on the Krishna; Andhra Pradesh when asked, now on the Telangana-Andhra Pradesh border.

44-004.r: Nagarjuna Sagar Multipurpose Project → River Krishna (Andhra Pradesh).

45-001.r: Hirakud Dam → Mahanadi, Odisha, 15 km from Sambalpur; main dam 4801 m long.

46-001.r: Jet streams → westerly (west to east) winds at about 8-15 km height, confirmed in World War II, 300-500 km/h. So A (easterly) false, R true.

46-002.r: Chambal dams → Gandhi Sagar (MP), Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan); Chambal rises at Janapav Hills, Mhow; joins Yamuna near Itawa.

46-003.r: Multi-state projects: Chambal (Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh) and Mayurakshi (West Bengal, Jharkhand); Hirakud → Odisha only; Sharavati → Karnataka only.
46-003.c: The book gives no single answer (*): both (a) Chambal and (b) Mayurakshi are shared by two states.

46-004.r: Gandhi Sagar Dam → first of four Chambal Valley dams; Mandsaur district, Madhya Pradesh; masonry gravity dam 62.17 m; power from 1960.

46-005.r: Not Chambal: Gobind Sagar (Bhakra-Nangal, Himachal) and Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar (Sonebhadra, UP). Chambal: Gandhi Sagar, Jawahar Sagar.
46-005.t: Don't confuse Gobind Sagar (Himachal, Bhakra) with Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar (Sonebhadra, Uttar Pradesh).
